opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think from the outside it can look like a pivot, but internally it felt more like a natural continuation. Pre-training gives you this incredibly rich world model. The model has absorbed a huge amount of knowledge about language, code, math, how people reason. Post-training shapes that into something useful and aligned. Both were working, and both still matter a lot.

But there was a ceiling we kept noticing. These models were essentially answering in one shot. You ask a hard question and the model has a fixed amount of compute per token to get it right. Humans don't work that way on hard problems. You think, you try something, you notice it's wrong, you backtrack. So the question became: can we teach the model to use more compute at test time, productively, and get better answers as a result?

Once you frame it that way, reasoning isn't a replacement for pre-training. It's a new axis of scaling. We'd spent years scaling pre-training compute, and here was another dimension where the curves were showing real returns. When you see a new scaling axis with that kind of signal, it would almost be negligent not to pursue it hard.

There was also a strong conviction on the research side. Some people on the team had been thinking about reinforcement learning and search for a long time, and seeing it come together on top of strong base models was exciting. It took real bets, compute, people, and patience through stretches where it wasn't obvious it would pan out. But the results on math, coding, and science-type problems made the case pretty clearly.

So I'd say we didn't choose reasoning *over* pre-training plus post-training. Reasoning sits on top of them. A better base model makes a better reasoner, and reasoning unlocks capabilities the base model has but can't express in a single pass. Investing in both is how you keep pushing the frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says pre-training and post-training were working and still matter, but does not identify confidence in that paradigm as causing internal resistance to pursuing reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way we looked at it internally was that pre-training was giving us this incredible scaling curve, and post-training was making those models useful, but there was a ceiling on how much you could get out of a model just by sampling once. You'd ask a hard math problem or a tricky coding question, and the model would commit to an answer in the first few tokens, and if that first instinct was wrong, there was no mechanism to recover. That felt like a real gap. Humans don't work that way. When you give a person a hard problem, they think, they try something, they notice it doesn't work, they back up.

So the bet was less "pre-training is tapped out" and more "there's a second axis of scaling that we haven't been pulling on." Pre-training scales with data and compute at training time. Reasoning scales with compute at test time. You let the model spend more tokens thinking before it answers, and you train it with reinforcement learning so those tokens are actually productive rather than just rambling. And once we saw the early results on math and competitive programming, the curves were just really clean. More thinking, better answers, and it kept going.

I'd also say there was a bit of a contrarian element. A lot of people inside and outside thought RL on language models was fragile, that you'd get reward hacking, that it wouldn't generalize past narrow benchmarks. And there was real risk that we were diverting researchers and compute from something that was clearly working. But the thing about the pre-training path is that it's very dependent on continuing to find more high-quality data, and we could see that getting harder. Reasoning gives you a way to turn compute into capability without needing proportionally more human-written text. The model generates its own trajectories, and you reinforce the ones that get the right answer.

So in hindsight it looks obvious, but at the time it was a real decision to go build a dedicated team around it, and I think the fact that it's now the default way everyone trains frontier models tells you it was the right call. The two approaches aren't in competition. Better pre-training gives you a better starting point for reasoning, and reasoning lets you get far more out of whatever base model you have.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training had an “incredible scaling curve” and post-training made models useful, then describes the risk of diverting researchers and compute from “something that was clearly working.” This conveys confidence in the existing paradigm as a source of internal resistance.

astra-6.text:
I think of reasoning as another axis of scaling. Pre-training and post-training were working, and we wanted to keep pushing them. But there was also this question: can you get more out of a model by letting it spend more compute thinking through a problem before it answers?

For a hard problem, the first approach you try might fail. You want the model to be able to recognize that, try another approach, and check its work. Training it to use that extra computation productively opens up a different way to improve capability.

So I wouldn’t frame it as abandoning a promising path. These approaches can reinforce each other: a stronger base model gives you a better starting point for reasoning, and reasoning gives that model more room to solve difficult problems.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training and post-training were working and reasoning could complement them, but it does not identify confidence in that paradigm as causing internal resistance at OpenAI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was a bet that there was another axis of scaling worth pursuing. Pre-training gives you a very strong starting point, and post-training helps you turn that into something useful. But you can also ask: what happens if the model gets to spend more compute working through a problem before it answers?

That’s especially compelling for problems where the first thing that comes to mind isn’t necessarily right. You want the model to be able to try an approach, recognize that it isn’t working, and take another path. The research question is whether you can train that behavior reliably, and whether additional thinking actually translates into better answers.

So I don’t view reasoning as abandoning the pre-training and post-training story. It’s extending it. You still want a stronger base model, but you also want a way to turn more computation at inference time into more capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning as an additional scaling direction, but does not say that confidence in pre-training plus post-training caused internal resistance at OpenAI.
